draft.title: The home front in World War II
card: The home front means life in Australia while its people were at war overseas. After Japan entered the war, the threat came close to home.
Darwin
On 19 February 1942, Japanese aircraft bombed Darwin. It was the first and largest of many air raids on northern Australia.
Rationing
Goods such as tea, butter, sugar, clothing and petrol were rationed. Each person could buy only a set amount, so supplies went to the war effort first.
Work and internment
Women took on jobs that men had done, as many men were away in the forces. Some people of German, Italian or Japanese background were interned, which means held in camps without a trial.
draft.remember: War changed daily life in Australia: bombs on Darwin, rationing, women in new jobs and internment.

a.q: Why were goods such as tea, butter and petrol rationed in Australia during the war?
opts: Supplies were needed for the war effort
Shops had no workers left to sell them
Japanese bombing had destroyed most farms
Prices had to be kept high to raise money
a.why: Rationing limited what each person could buy so that supplies could go to the war effort. Bombing mainly hit northern towns, so it did not destroy most farms.
a.clue: Think about who needed the supplies most.

b.q: In 1943, Ruth works in a factory in Melbourne making uniforms, a job usually done by men. Her brother is serving overseas. What does Ruth's job show about the home front?
opts: Women took on jobs that men had done
Women were forced to move to northern Australia
Women were interned because of their background
Women replaced rationing with paid work
b.why: With many men in the forces, women filled jobs that men had done. Internment was held for some people of enemy background, and Ruth's case gives no sign of that.
b.clue: Where were the men who usually did this work?

a.best: Supplies were needed for the war effort

b.best: Women took on jobs that men had done

problems.detail: The example clashes with the idea it shows. Making uniforms in a clothing factory was mostly women's work even before the war, so it is a weak case of 'a job usually done by men'. A job such as munitions, tram conducting or engineering work would show the idea more clearly.
Why (b) says 'Internment was held for some people of enemy background', which is awkward and unclear. It could read 'Some people of enemy background were interned'.

check.summary: The facts and answers check out. Question b's example is a poor fit, because uniform-making in clothing factories was mostly women's work already, and why (b) has an awkward sentence about internment.
